Solomon Asch. Solomon Asch was a Polish-American social psychologist famous for the Asch Conformity Experiments, a series of studies conducted in the nineteen fifties that revealed the extraordinary power of group pressure to shape individual judgment and behavior, even when that pressure contradicts objective reality.

Asch conducted the conformity experiments from nineteen fifty-one to nineteen fifty-five, showing that about seventy-five percent of participants conformed to obviously incorrect group answers at least once. The experimental setup was deceptively simple. Participants were asked to judge the length of lines on a card, a task anyone can do accurately. They judged the lines alongside confederates, actors pretending to be fellow participants, who gave incorrect answers. What made this powerful was that participants knew their answers were wrong. They could see clearly that the line length didn't match what the group was saying. Yet they conformed anyway to avoid social rejection, demonstrating that social pressure overrides perceptual reality for most people. They denied the evidence of their own eyes.

Asch found that conformity increased with group size, up to about three or four people, and then plateaued even with larger groups. Conformity decreased dramatically when even one other person broke the group consensus and gave the correct answer. That single dissenter was enough to free people from the pressure to conform. The experiments revealed conformity as a normal, widespread phenomenon rather than a personality defect or sign of weakness. It wasn't the socially anxious or insecure who conformed. Many intelligent, confident people conformed to avoid social disapproval. The power of the group affected ordinary people in ordinary circumstances.

His work became foundational to understanding conformity, groupthink, and the limits of individual agency in social contexts. It became a touchstone for later research on obedience, particularly Stanley Milgram's work on obedience to authority, and is frequently cited in discussions of groupthink, jury dynamics, and collective delusion.
